Lessons.Title: Interpret Diagrams
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L17 compares fraction products of positive amounts to baseline factors, matches multiple fractions to publisher DIAGRAMS, and orders named runners without knowing Priya's numeric original distance.

Warm-up original Estimation Exploration5/3×9625. Multiplier5/3>1 so product is GREATER than9625, and approximate location may be discussed; student low/about-right/high estimates are not uniquely keyed.

Activity1 Match the Diagram original four expressions2/7×3=6/7<3,9/7×3=27/7>3,2/7×5=10/7<5,9/7×5=45/7>5. Source diagrams are teacher-scored, and the exact interpretation needs 7 equal pieces of each original whole. Prior independently invented2/5 and6/5 examples are not printed source tasks.

Activity2 Who Ran Farther original baseline Priya distance P>0. Jada2P, Han6/7P, Clare14/8P=7/4P and Mai3/5P. Ordered shortest to longest: Mai,Han,Priya,Clare,Jada. Farther than Priya are Jada and Clare; shorter are Han and Mai. Original source asks mapping INITIALS to positions of a number line with one missing; teacher assesses actual publisher diagram.

Exact selected practice includes source expressions and ordering; original figure matching, shaded units and warm-up open estimates are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED, as is any unrecovered publisher Cool-down. Edulytiks independent teacher Cool-down tests alternate ratios.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: MATCH fraction multiplication expressions with fraction-area diagrams and relative number-line positions, then compare products with a selected positive original factor. The 2021 source also asks students to compare a runner's unknown baseline distance with several fractions of it, without computing the unknown distance.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: take an original four-unit line segment. Mark a factor 3/4 of the four units to the LEFT of the four-unit endpoint, and 5/4 of it to the RIGHT. Explain why the relative position alone shows the inequality, even without identifying an exact length.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original matching task: expressions 2/5×3, 6/5×3, 2/5×5 and6/5×5 should be matched to two descriptions: a shaded two-fifths of 3 or5 equal wholes, and a sixth-fifths extension after a full original amount. Compare 2/5×3<3,6/5×3>3, and analogous inequalities for5. The student draws or selects consistent shaded diagrams and corresponding number-line points.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — unknown runner distance: let P be a positive unknown distance. Student A ran three fifths of P, B ran seven fourths of P, C ran twice P, D ran five sixths of P. Without computing P, order A < D < original P < B < C. Explain why multiplying each factor by the same positive P preserves ordering.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: matching abstract diagrams, placing an unknown-runner distance on a number line, and explaining why the factor size determines ordering are teacher-reviewed; numeric fractions alone are insufficient to complete the source activity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Match fraction and area model
KeyConcepts.Definition: An area of a/b of a rectangle represents a fraction of the SAME original quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: The shaded part must refer to three original units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare product to factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying a positive amount by a factor below one decreases it; above one increases it.
KeyConcepts.Example: No exact product calculation required for direction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown positive baseline
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inequality between positive multipliers is maintained after multiplying each by unknown P>0.
KeyConcepts.Example: The product order follows factor order.

Lessons.Title: Compare Without Multiplying
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L18 compares products by asking whether multiplier is below, equal or above one, using approximate SOURCE number lines and an UNKNOWN positive quantity A. Students are not required to compute exact products for every inequality.
Warm-up original Notice and Wonder uses 2/3×5, a value below5, with source number-line illustration and student insights teacher reviewed.

Activity1 Approximate Location PartnerA original2/5×12=24/5,5/3×12=20,7/7×12=12. PartnerB original4/7×12=48/7,8/5×12=96/5,9/9×12=12. Partner draws each position on the publisher line; original axis artwork and spatial precision remain teacher reviewed.

Activity1 other source boxes n/11×12>12 requires n>11 (e.g12); n/15×12=12 requires n15; 13/d×12<12 requires denominator d>13 (e.g14). The source admits many integer values for inequalities; exact choices are illustrative only, not a universal key.

Activity2 An Unknown Number original locations1/4 A<A,2A>A,13/8 A>A and2/3 A<A assuming source positive A. Printed comparisons13/8×11/39>11/39 and2/3×17/53<17/53. Teacher assesses source number line labels and explanation.

Prior fictional3/5×12 tasks are valid Edulytiks extensions only. Selected numeric family covers source expressions and bounded relational rules but not student-drawn coordinate placement and free-choice blanks.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: place fraction products at approximate positions on a number line and generalize comparisons to ANY positive amount A, including fractional A. In the source, students choose numbers to make inequalities true and explain why the rule works without arithmetic evaluation.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: put 1/3×12 and4/3×12 on opposite sides of12 using an original zero-to-twenty number line. An estimate based on the factor relationship to one is enough to determine direction before exact plotting.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — fractions of twelve: plot 3/5×12=36/5, 7/7×12=12, and5/4×12=15; the third is right of12 and the first left. Choose an integer numerator n in n/11×12>12, requiring n>11; choose n/15×12=12, requiring n=15; and choose denominator d in 13/d×12<12, requiring d>13 for positive integer d.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — unknown A: suppose A is any positive fraction on the number line. Place (1/4)A,(2/3)A,A,(13/8)A,2A in increasing order. Test examples A=3/5 and A=7/9 without claiming the ordering needs numerical values; explain why it is valid for positive A.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: exact comparisons and inequality choices may be checked mechanically, but the source asks learners to plot relative location, state a rule with the needed positivity condition and justify the choice of unknown numerators and denominators; teacher review is required.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction comparisons without computing
KeyConcepts.Definition: For A>0, fA<A when0<f<1, and fA>A when f>1.
KeyConcepts.Example: The reference number A can be a whole or a fraction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Numerator/denominator inequality
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive fraction n/d is greater than one if n>d, equal if n=d, smaller if n<d.

KeyConcepts.Title: Relative number-line location
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use a correct increasing scale and estimate positions by the factor.

Lessons.Title: Compare to 1 PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L19 uses distributive law to show why a factor above1 ADDS a positive fraction of baseline, a factor below1 SUBTRACTS a positive fraction. Original number-line matching of equivalent expressions requires teacher review.
Warm-up source15/14×23/30=23/28, and because15/14>1, resulting23/28 is GREATER than source second factor23/30. The source asks what pupils notice, not just a long fraction multiplication.

Activity1 Compare Fraction Products on the Number Line printed expressions2/5×4/3=8/15,3/4×5/2=15/8 and4/3×5/2=10/3. Matched forms(1+1/3)×5/2=10/3,(1−3/5)×4/3=8/15 and(1−1/4)×5/2=15/8. Teacher assesses original A/B/C diagram matching and why different syntaxes describe same positions.

Activity2 True Statement original four transformations(1−2/5)×4/7=12/35 <4/7,(1+1/5)×4/7=24/35 >4/7,(1−3/8)×4/7=5/14 <4/7,(1+1/8)×4/7=9/14 >4/7. Students must rewrite each as base4/7 plus/minus a smaller positive product and explain the signs.

Previous independently-authored3/5×4/7 and6/5×4/7 examples remain optional Edulytiks extensions only. Numeric selected Practice covers original products but not source picture positions, distributed proof and original gated Cool-down.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: rewrite factors above or below one as 1 plus a positive part or 1 minus a positive part, then use distributivity to EXPLAIN why products change size. The source matches pairs of fraction expressions to the same number-line result and requires qualitative comparisons with a common second factor.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare0.9×4/7 and1.1×4/7. Both refer to the same positive baseline4/7, but one removes a tenth of it and the other adds a tenth. Do not compute decimals first; interpret sign and size.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original expression matching: 3/5×4/7=(1−2/5)×4/7=4/7−(2/5×4/7). Both match a position BELOW4/7. Conversely6/5×4/7=(1+1/5)×4/7=4/7+(1/5×4/7), above4/7. The learner must match equivalent expression cards and explain why two different syntactic descriptions depict the same selected number-line point.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — generalize by expansion: (1−1/4)×5/6=5/6−(1/4×5/6)<5/6; (1+3/8)×5/6=5/6+(3/8×5/6)>5/6. Ask students to produce another pair of valid positive fractions and defend why subtraction of a positive quantity shrinks a product, while addition increases it.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: matching published diagrams, using the distributive property as explanation and partner mathematical critique are teacher-judged. A machine may check exact fraction equivalence, not whether the student produced a valid source-like representation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribute a fraction below one
KeyConcepts.Definition: Write f=1−h with h>0, then fA=A−hA<A for A>0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribute a fraction above one
KeyConcepts.Definition: Write f=1+h with h>0, then fA=A+hA>A.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent multiplication expressions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction and its one-plus/one-minus decomposition may produce the same location.
KeyConcepts.Example: Expression matching must retain the same baseline.

Lessons.Title: Will it Always Work? (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L20 OPTIONAL proves fraction product comparisons without multiplying large numerators/denominators and checks when a general rule is valid for POSITIVE fractions. For baseline zero or negative (outside current Grade5 task assumptions), strict inequalities need different conditions, so explanations must not claim unconditional universality.
Warm-up original TRUE/FALSE3/4=1−1/4 TRUE,(1−1/4)×9=9−(1/4×9) TRUE,(1+1/4)×7=7+1/4 FALSE because correct distribution also multiplies the extra1/4 by7.

Activity1 True Statements original comparisons567 <345×567,4/5×851 <851,1/4 =5/5×1/4,103/104 >(103/104)×(103/104),99/8×23/22 >99/8,10/10×1/2=1/2,100/7×9/13 >9/13. Explain each by positive baseline and the other factor compared with1.

Activity2 Andre's two printed rules: multiplying a positive fraction by a factor LESS THAN1 makes smaller result, multiplying by a factor GREATER THAN1 makes larger. Teacher checks the missing positivity assumptions, distributive proof, examples and diagrams. No sole sequence of seven signs replaces Andre's general argument.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — inequalities with large numbers: decide 3/5×742<742, 127/128×311<311 and13/12×49>49. Compare also1/4×4/4=1/4 and7/7×1/2=1/2 for factors exactly one; the latter examples require EQUALITY rather than a strict inequality.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — evaluate a student's proposed rule: for a positive fraction x, a factor f greater than one makes fx>x, a factor between zero and one makes fx<x, and f=1 preserves x. Prove using f=1+h or1−h, noting h>0. Clarify zero baseline would make all products zero and a negative baseline would reverse the strict comparison, outside the source's positive-fraction focus.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: proof-writing, poster/gallery explanation, reasoned critique of an 'always' statement and edge-case precision require human review, while selected exact comparisons are supporting numerical checks.

Lessons.Title: Weekend Investigation (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: collect ACTUAL class observations about a bounded amount of free time, define mutually understandable categories, convert minutes into fractional hours, and construct and analyze line plots for each selected category. This optional lesson is a real-data modeling activity: invented source-like counts must NOT be treated as student submissions.

Warm-up: reason that 15 minutes=1/4 hour,30 minutes=1/2 hour,45 minutes=3/4 hour and90 minutes=1 1/2 hours. Ask pupils whether a category such as reading should include audiobooks and whether a socializing category overlaps recreation; category definitions matter for interpretation.

Activity 1 — first-party fictional demonstration ONLY: six pretend students report reading for 0,15,30,30,45,60 minutes during a two-hour break. Convert to hours:0,1/4,1/2,1/2,3/4,1. Place exactly two marks at one half and one at each other tick. In authentic instruction, learners define categories and enter their own observed or planned durations; software must not generate substitute class data.

Activity 2 — analyze that *fictional* plot: total reading duration0+1/4+1/2+1/2+3/4+1=3 hours for six students. The range is one hour; five out of six students spent less than one hour, or5/6 of the group, and one student spent exactly one hour. Students pose three original questions about a real class plot and discuss any sampling or reporting biases before drawing conclusions.

Teacher boundary: defining categories, collecting real data, visually plotting equal unit increments, forming multiple questions and discussing uncertainty are teacher-reviewed. No single fixed total or line plot can automatically certify that the source's genuine data-collection project was completed; support privacy-safe aggregated classroom data.

KeyConcepts.Title: Minutes convert to fractional hours
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide minutes by60 to obtain hours.
KeyConcepts.Example: Fractions refer to a 60-minute whole hour.

KeyConcepts.Title: Line-plot counts represent observations
KeyConcepts.Definition: One X should correspond to exactly one submitted data value at the labeled fractional tick.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two students with30 minutes produce two X marks at1/2 hour.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not mistake an X as 1/2 a student.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sampling and categories matter
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mathematical graph is meaningful only with clear definitions and authentic data.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Six fictional readings sum3h; real classroom data may differ.

WorkedExamples.Check: Six observations remain exactly six X marks.

WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of the six fictional observations is strictly below one hour?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction/number-line reasoning with teacher-reviewed explanation and exact numeric subcheck.
Steps: Count five observations below one hour:0,1/4,1/2,1/2,3/4.

WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies strict inequality and actual original count.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Present a fabricated dataset as genuine student's collected data
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source requires observations made by students or their class.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Clearly label examples fictional and collect real submissions separately.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confuse an observation's fraction of an hour with a fraction of students
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One is a time quantity; the other compares counts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label units on plot positions and denominators in count fractions.

SummaryPoints: Convert minute totals to hours and plot observations on equal fractional ticks.
A real data investigation requires defined categories and actual student records.
Teacher reviews interpretation and data authenticity; arithmetic alone is insufficient.
